doc.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Learning guitar from Bill Johnson's loaned instrument
summary: Bill Johnson loaned him a guitar and showed him four basic chords, which Barker mapped onto his ukulele knowledge.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Luis Russell’s man. Yeah, Bill, that’s who. I can’t think of his last name. He had a guitar, two guitars on a stand when I saw him. So he say, “Go ask him to loan you a guitar.” Your uncle’s in the band. He knows you. You ain’t going to run away with the guitar. So I went to see him, and he loaned me the guitar. He told me, he said, “You see the first four strings on that guitar. It’s the same as the ukulele. Now you come there and you fool around, and I’ll show you the different keys.” He showed me the C chord, he showed a C7 chord, the C minor chord, and that’s all your fingering on the guitar. I’m familiar with the ukulele, so [expletive deleted]. I said, “Yeah.” So I sit on the bandstand, and I had liberty to play muted or not, ’til I get with, get the construction of the chords. That’s how I started playing the guitar. Had a few formal lessons, but not . . .
Who taught you lessons when you took them?

Harry White [Bill Johnson] showed me them four basic things. The rest I did, I bought me some books, and Bernard Addison gave me some pointers, but he was always in a hurry. I asked different guitar players. I went by their house, and they showed me things. Veterans, guitar players.
So pretty much you were learning how to play the role of rhythm guitar at the time.
That’s right. Rhythm guitar. That’s what they had.
